h1: Day To Day As a UI/UX Designer

paragraphs: As a UI/UX designer, no two days are exactly the same. The constantly evolving nature of the design industry means that there is always something new to learn, something new to try, and something new to improve upon.

One of the key tasks of a UI/UX designer is conducting user research. This involves gathering data on how users interact with a product or service, and using that information to inform design decisions. This can take many forms, from interviews and surveys to usability testing and analytics analysis.

Once the data has been collected, a UI/UX designer will use it to create user personas and user flows. These help to define the key characteristics and goals of the users, and to map out the steps they will take to achieve their goals. This information is then used to create wireframes and prototypes, which are early versions of the design that can be tested and refined.

Another important aspect of a UI/UX designer’s day is collaboration. Working closely with other designers, product managers, and developers is essential to ensure that everyone is on the same page, and that the design meets the needs of the users and the goals of the project. This might involve regular meetings, design reviews, and the sharing of design assets and documentation.

Of course, no design process is complete without testing and iteration. UI/UX designers need to be prepared to test their designs with users, gather feedback, and make changes based on the results. This can be a time-consuming process, but it is essential to creating a user-centered design that meets the needs of the users.

In short, a day in the life of a UI/UX designer is a mix of user research, design, collaboration, and testing. It’s a challenging and rewarding role that requires a combination of creativity, technical skill, and empathy for the users. But the end result, a product or service that delights and satisfies its users, is more than worth the effort.

h1: Improving Your Collaboration Skills As a UI/UX Designer

paragraphs: As a UI/UX designer, collaboration is a key part of your job. Whether you’re working in a small team or a large organization, the ability to communicate and work effectively with others is essential to creating great user experiences.
But how can you improve your collaboration skills as a UI/UX designer? Here are a few tips:

Be open to feedback: As a designer, it can be easy to become attached to your ideas and designs. But it’s important to remember that collaboration is about working together to create the best possible solution, not about defending your own ideas at all costs. Be open to feedback from others, and be willing to make changes based on that feedback.

Communicate clearly: Good communication is the foundation of any successful collaboration. Make sure to clearly explain your design decisions and the reasoning behind them. Be open to questions and suggestions, and be willing to listen to the perspectives of others.
Be proactive: Don’t wait for others to come to you with ideas or feedback. Take the initiative to seek out input from others, and be proactive in suggesting solutions and improvements.

Be flexible: Collaboration often involves compromise, so be prepared to adapt your ideas and designs based on the input of others. Remember that the goal is to create the best possible user experience, not to stubbornly stick to your original ideas.

Keep an open mind: Collaboration is about more than just agreeing with others. It’s about bringing together different perspectives and ideas to create something new and better. Keep an open mind and be willing to consider new ideas, even if they are different from your own.

By improving your collaboration skills as a UI/UX designer, you can create better user experiences and work more effectively with your team. Remember to be open to feedback, communicate clearly, be proactive, be flexible, and keep an open mind. With these skills, you can be an invaluable part of any design team.

h1: Getting Laid Off Was Not The End Of Your Job Careers

paragraphs: Getting laid off can be a difficult and stressful experience. It can be tempting to feel like your job prospects are over, but it’s important to remember that getting laid off is not the end of your career. In fact, it can be an opportunity to reassess your career goals and make a change if necessary.

Getting laid off can be seen as a chance to take stock of your career and make changes if needed. It can be a time to reassess your goals and consider new opportunities that you may not have considered before. For example, if you were laid off from a job in a field that you weren’t particularly passionate about, getting laid off can give you the chance to explore other careers that align more closely with your interests and values.In addition to giving you the opportunity to explore new career paths, getting laid off can also be a chance to upskill and learn new things. Many employers are looking for candidates with a diverse range of skills and experience, and taking the time to learn new skills can make you a more competitive job candidate. There are many online courses, workshops, and other resources available that can help you learn new skills and advance your career.

If you’ve been laid off, it’s important to stay positive and proactive. Here are a few tips to help you bounce back and get back on track with your job search:1. Update your resume: Take the time to review and update your resume to highlight your skills and experience. Be sure to include any new skills or certifications that you’ve acquired since your last job.2. Network: Networking is an important part of any job search, and it can be especially helpful after getting laid off. Connect with friends, family, and professional organizations to let them know that you’re looking for work and see if they know of any job opportunities.3. Look for new job opportunities: Use job search websites and other resources to find job openings that align with your skills and experience. Be sure to tailor your applications to each specific job to increase your chances of getting hired.4. Seek support: Getting laid off can be a difficult experience, and it’s important to seek support from friends, family, and professional organizations during this time. They can provide emotional support and advice to help you through this difficult time.

ConclusionGetting laid off is not the end of your career. It can be a difficult and stressful experience, but it can also be an opportunity to reassess your career goals and explore new opportunities. By staying positive, networking, and looking for new job opportunities, you can bounce back and get back on track with your career.

h1: How to Understand Better Your User?

paragraphs: As designers, it’s essential that we have a deep understanding of the people who will be using our products. But how do we go about gaining that understanding? In this post, we’ll explore some strategies and techniques for getting to know your users on a deeper level.One of the most effective ways to understand your users is to simply talk to them. This can be done through methods such as in-depth interviews, focus groups, or user testing sessions. These types of conversations can provide valuable insights into the needs, goals, and motivations of your users, as well as their experiences with your product.Another useful approach is to observe your users in their natural environment. This can be done through field studies or user shadowing, where you follow users as they go about their day and observe how they interact with your product and others. This can give you a better understanding of the context in which your product is used, and help you identify any pain points or areas for improvement.Data analysis is another key tool for understanding your users.By analyzing usage data and other metrics, you can get a sense of how users are interacting with your product and identify trends or patterns. This can be especially useful for understanding how different groups of users engage with your product differently.Finally, it’s important to remember that user understanding is an ongoing process. As your product evolves and your users’ needs change, it’s important to continuously gather and analyze data to ensure that you’re meeting their needs.

In conclusion, understanding your users is an essential part of the design process. By using a combination of conversations, observations, and data analysis, you can gain valuable insights into the needs and motivations of your users, and use that knowledge to inform the design of your product.

h1: Why is UX Research So Important?

paragraphs: If you’re involved in the design of digital products, you’ve probably heard the term “UX research” thrown around. But why is it so important? In this post, we’ll explore the significance of UX research and how it can benefit your product and your users.

At its core, UX research is the process of studying how people interact with and experience a product. It’s all about understanding the needs, behaviors, and motivations of the users of a product, and using that knowledge to inform the design and development process.
So, why is UX research so important? There are several reasons.

First and foremost, it helps to ensure that the product you’re designing is actually useful and usable for your target audience. By understanding the needs and goals of your users, you can create a product that meets their expectations and helps them achieve their objectives. This is especially important in today’s crowded and competitive market, where users have many options to choose from. If your product isn’t meeting their needs, they’re likely to look elsewhere.

In addition, UX research can help to identify potential problems or barriers to use that might not be immediately apparent. By studying how users interact with a product, you can identify pain points and areas for improvement, and make changes to address those issues. This can help to ensure that your product is as user-friendly as possible, which can translate into higher satisfaction and loyalty from your users.

Finally, UX research can help to create a more cohesive and consistent user experience. By understanding the expectations and preferences of your users, you can design a product that feels intuitive and natural to them, rather than one that is confusing or frustrating. This can help to build trust and credibility with your users, and contribute to their overall satisfaction with your product.

In short, UX research is an essential part of the design process, helping to ensure that the products we create are useful, usable, and enjoyable for our users. If you’re not already incorporating UX research into your design process, we highly recommend giving it a try, you might be surprised at the insights and benefits it can provide.

h1: What, Why, and When Use Evaluative Research?

paragraphs: So, what is evaluative research? Evaluative research is a type of UX research that focuses on testing and evaluating existing designs or prototypes, rather than exploring and generating new ideas. It’s all about gathering feedback and data on how well a product is meeting the needs of its users, and typically involves more structured and focused methods, such as usability testing, A/B testing, and surveys.

Evaluative research is typically used later in the design process, when you have a more concrete design or prototype that you want to test and refine. It can be especially useful for identifying areas of improvement and making informed design decisions.
So, why is evaluative research important? There are several reasons.

First and foremost, it helps to ensure that the product you’re designing is actually useful and usable for your target audience. By gathering feedback and data on how well the product is meeting the needs of its users, you can identify any issues or problems, and make changes to address them.

In addition, evaluative research can help to identify areas of differentiation or competitive advantage. By comparing your product to similar products on the market, you can identify unique features or benefits that set it apart.

Finally, evaluative research can help to build credibility and trust with your users. By demonstrating that you are actively listening to and responding to their feedback, you can build a sense of trust and rapport with your users.

In conclusion, evaluative research is an important part of the design process, helping to ensure that the products we create are effective and meet the needs of our users. If you’re not already incorporating evaluative research into your design process, we highly recommend giving it a try, it can provide valuable insights and help to improve the overall user experience.

So, what is generative research? Generative research is a type of UX research that focuses on exploring and generating ideas, rather than testing and evaluating existing ones. It’s all about gathering insights and inspiration that can inform the design process, and typically involves more open-ended and exploratory methods, such as in-depth interviews, focus groups, and brainstorming sessions.

Generative research is typically used early in the design process, when you’re trying to identify new opportunities or directions for your product. It can be especially useful for gathering insights and ideas from potential users, and can help to inform the development of personas, user stories, and other design artifacts.

First and foremost, it helps to ensure that the product you’re designing is based on a solid understanding of your users’ needs and goals. By gathering insights and ideas from potential users, you can create a product that meets their expectations and helps them achieve their objectives.

In addition, generative research can help to identify untapped opportunities and areas for innovation. By exploring new ideas and approaches, you can uncover new ways to solve problems or meet the needs of your users.

Finally, generative research can help to build a shared understanding and vision among your team. By involving stakeholders and team members in the exploration and ideation process, you can create a shared understanding of the product and its potential impact.

In conclusion, generative research is an important part of the design process, helping to ensure that the products we create are based on a deep understanding of our users’ needs and goals, and are informed by a range of ideas and perspectives. paragraphs: If you’re involved in the design of digital products, you know that UX research is an essential part of the process. But with so many different research methods available, it can be overwhelming to know which one to use. In this post, we’ll explore some of the most common UX research methods and how to choose the right one for your project.

One of the most widely used UX research methods is usability testing. This involves observing users as they interact with a product, and collecting data on their behaviors, preferences, and any issues they encounter. Usability testing is often conducted in a controlled environment, such as a lab, and can be either moderated, where a researcher observes and interacts with the user, or unmoderated, where the user completes tasks on their own.

Another common UX research method is in-depth interviews. This involves one-on-one conversations with users, in which the researcher asks open-ended questions to gather insights into their experiences, behaviors, and motivations. In-depth interviews are a great way to get a deep understanding of a user’s perspective and can be especially useful for gathering qualitative data.

Focus groups are another popular UX research method, involving small groups of users who come together to discuss and provide feedback on a product. Focus groups can be an effective way to gather a range of perspectives and identify common themes or trends.

Data analysis is another important UX research method, involving the collection and analysis of data from various sources, such as usage logs, customer feedback, or surveys. Data analysis can provide valuable insights into how users are interacting with a product, and can be especially useful for identifying trends or patterns.

When choosing a UX research method, it’s important to consider your research objectives, target audience, and resources. Different methods are better suited to different types of research, and it’s important to choose the one that will best help you to achieve your goals.

In conclusion, there are many different UX research methods available, and choosing the right one for your project can be challenging. By considering your research objectives, target audience, and resources, you can select the most appropriate method for your needs.

h1: The Benefits of User Experience Research

paragraphs: UX research is the practice of studying and understanding the behaviors, needs, and attitudes of people who use a product or service. This type of research is critical for the design and development of products and services that are user-friendly, effective, and enjoyable to use.

One major benefit of UX research is that it helps to improve the user experience of a product or service. By understanding how people use and interact with a product, designers and developers can identify areas for improvement and make necessary changes to create a better user experience. UX research can also help to identify user needs and preferences, which can be used to inform the design and development process.

Another benefit of UX research is that it helps to identify and fix usability issues. Usability refers to the ease of use and effectiveness of a product or service. By conducting UX research, designers and developers can identify areas where users are struggling to use the product and make necessary changes to improve usability.

In addition, UX research can also help to increase customer satisfaction and loyalty. When a product or service is designed with the user in mind and meets their needs and preferences, customers are more likely to be satisfied and continue using the product. This can lead to increased customer loyalty and positive word-of-mouth marketing.

UX research can also have financial benefits for a company. By identifying and addressing usability issues, a company can save money by reducing the need for customer support and increasing the efficiency of its products or services. Additionally, a better user experience can lead to increased sales and customer loyalty, which can result in increased profits.

In conclusion, UX research is a valuable tool for the design and development of products and services. It can help to improve the user experience, identify and fix usability issues, increase customer satisfaction and loyalty, and have financial benefits for a company. If you are involved in the design or development of products or services, consider incorporating UX research into your process to help create user-friendly and successful products.

paragraphs: Context is an essential element of design that should not be overlooked. It refers to the surroundings, circumstances, and environment in which a design is used. Understanding the context in which a design will be used is crucial in creating a successful and effective product or service.

One reason why context is so important in design is that it can greatly affect the way a design is perceived and used. For example, a design that works well in one context may not be as effective in a different context. A design that is intuitive and easy to use in a familiar environment may be confusing and frustrating in a new or unfamiliar context.

Another reason why context is important in design is that it can influence the usability and accessibility of a design. A design that is not tailored to the specific needs and abilities of its intended users may not be effective or usable for those users. For example, a design that is not accessible for users with disabilities may exclude a significant portion of the intended audience.

In summary, context is an essential consideration in design that should not be overlooked. By understanding the context in which a design will be used, designers can create products and services that are more effective, usable, and accessible for their intended users.

h1: 5 Tips to Do Focus Group Discussions Effectively

paragraphs: Focus group discussions are a useful technique for gathering insights and feedback from a group of users in UX research. However, running an effective focus group discussion requires careful planning and facilitation.
Here are some tips for conducting an effective focus group discussion:

Define the focus and objectives: Clearly define the focus and objectives of the discussion, and create a list of questions to guide the conversation. This will help ensure that the discussion stays on track and is relevant to the research objectives.

Choose the right participants: Select a diverse group of participants who represent the target audience for the product or service being researched. Make sure to also consider any necessary demographics, such as age, gender, and location.

Create a comfortable and welcoming environment: The atmosphere of the focus group discussion should be welcoming and comfortable for all participants. Consider factors such as the size of the room, seating arrangements, and refreshments.

Facilitate the discussion: As the facilitator, it’s important to encourage open and honest communication from all participants. Avoid leading the conversation or interrupting participants, and instead, allow them to express their thoughts and opinions freely.

Record and transcribe the discussion: It’s important to record the focus group discussion for later analysis. This can be done through audio or video recording, or through detailed notes taken by the facilitator or a transcriptionist.
By following these tips, designers can effectively conduct focus group discussions and gather valuable insights for their UX research.

h1: A Good Way to Test and Validate the Concept in UX Research

paragraphs: UX research is a crucial aspect of the design process, as it helps designers understand the needs and behaviors of their target audience. One important step in UX research is concept testing, which involves evaluating the feasibility and appeal of a design concept.

There are several ways to test and validate a concept in UX research. One effective method is to conduct usability testing, in which users are asked to perform specific tasks using the prototype of the concept. This can help designers identify any issues or obstacles that users may encounter, and make necessary adjustments to the design.

Another useful technique is focus group testing, in which a group of users is brought together to discuss and provide feedback on the concept. This can be a valuable source of insights and ideas, as it allows designers to gather a diverse range of perspectives and opinions.

Another way to test and validate a concept is through A/B testing, in which two versions of the concept are presented to users and the one that performs better is chosen. This can be particularly useful for determining which design elements are most effective at meeting user needs.

In addition to these methods, designers can also conduct interviews and surveys to gather more in-depth insights into user attitudes and behaviors. This can help designers understand the motivations and pain points of their target audience, and design a concept that meets their needs.

Overall, there are many different ways to test and validate a concept in UX research. By using a combination of these methods, designers can ensure that their designs are well-researched and user-centered, resulting in a better overall user experience.

h1: 5 Tips for Remote User Interviews in UX Research Effectively

paragraphs: Conducting user interviews is an important aspect of UX research, as it allows designers to gather valuable insights and feedback from their target audience. While in-person interviews can be effective, they may not always be feasible due to various constraints such as geography or the current pandemic situation.
Fortunately, there are several ways to conduct effective remote user interviews in UX research. Here are some tips to keep in mind:
There are many tools available for conducting remote interviews, such as Zoom, Skype, and Google Meet. Choose a tool that is reliable and allows for smooth audio and video communication.
Before the interview, define the goals and objectives of the interview, and create a list of questions to guide the conversation. This will help ensure that the interview is focused and productive.

Prepare the user:Make sure to provide clear instructions to the user on how to prepare for the interview, including any technical requirements. It’s also important to set the right expectations and let the user know what to expect during the interview.

Create a comfortable environment: Encourage the user to create a comfortable and quiet environment for the interview. This will help them feel at ease and more willing to share their thoughts and opinions.

Pay attention to body language and tone: While remote interviews may lack in-person cues such as facial expressions and body language, it’s still important to pay attention to the user’s tone and any other nonverbal cues. This can help designers better understand the user’s perspective and emotions.
By following these tips, designers can effectively conduct remote user interviews and gather valuable insights for their UX research.

h1: 20 Common Product Design Terms You Need to Know

paragraphs: Product design is a complex field that involves creating and developing new products that meet the needs and wants of consumers. Whether you’re a designer, engineer, marketer, or entrepreneur, it’s important to have a strong understanding of the various terms and concepts that are commonly used in the product design process.
Here are 20 common product design terms you need to know:
Aesthetics: The visual appearance or style of a product.
A/B testing: A method of comparing two versions of a product to see which performs better.
Customer journey: The complete set of interactions and experiences a customer has with a product or service.
Design brief: A document that outlines the goals and objectives of a design project.
Design thinking: A creative approach to problem-solving that involves empathizing with users, defining problems, ideating solutions, prototyping, and testing.
Empathy map: A visual representation of a user’s thoughts, feelings, and actions.
Feasibility study: An analysis of whether a product idea is viable from a technical, financial, and market perspective.
Human-centered design: A design approach that focuses on understanding and meeting the needs of users.
Ideation: The process of generating and developing ideas.
Iterative design: A design process that involves continuously refining and improving a product through multiple cycles of prototyping and testing.
MVP (Minimum Viable Product): A product with the minimum set of features necessary to satisfy early customers and gather feedback for further development.
Personas: Fictional characters that represent different types of users and their needs and goals.
Prototyping: The process of creating a physical or digital model of a product to test and refine its design.
User experience (UX): The overall experience of a user when interacting with a product, including usability, accessibility, and enjoyment.
User interface (UI): The way a user interacts with a product, including the buttons, controls, and visual design.
User research: The process of collecting and analyzing data about users to inform design decisions.
Usability: The ease with which a user can learn and use a product.
User testing: The process of evaluating a product by having real users try it out and provide feedback.
Wireframing: The process of creating a basic visual layout of a product’s user interface.
Accessibility: The degree to which a product is easy to use and navigate by people with disabilities.
That’s all 20 product design terms that might you don’t know before. Thank for reading this article.

h1: 10 Most Common UX Design Mistakes that Startups Make

paragraphs: As a startup, it’s important to prioritize user experience (UX) in order to create products that are intuitive, easy to use, and enjoyable for your customers. However, it’s easy to make mistakes when it comes to UX design, especially if you’re working with limited resources or under tight deadlines.
Here are the 10 most common UX design mistakes that startups make:
Failing to understand user needs: It’s important to conduct thorough user research to understand the needs, goals, and pain points of your target audience.
Ignoring mobile users: With the increasing popularity of smartphones and tablets, it’s important to design for mobile users as well as desktop users.
Not having a clear value proposition: Make sure your product clearly communicates its value to potential users.
Complex navigation:Keep your navigation simple and intuitive to make it easy for users to find what they’re looking for.
Poor layout:Make sure your layout is visually appealing and easy to read, with plenty of white space and clear headings.
Lack of consistency:Use consistent design elements throughout your product to create a cohesive user experience.
Overloading users with information: Don’t try to cram too much information onto a single page. Use clear headings and bullet points to break up text and make it easy to scan.
Not testing your design: It’s important to test your design with real users to identify any usability issues and make improvements.
Neglecting accessibility: Make sure your product is accessible to users with disabilities by following web accessibility guidelines.
Ignoring user feedback: Make sure to gather and incorporate feedback from users to continuously improve your product’s UX.
By avoiding these common UX design mistakes, you can create a product that meets the needs of your users and helps your startup succeed.

paragraphs: Empathy is one of the most important skills a UI/UX designer can have. It allows us to understand and relate to our users, which in turn helps us to create better, more user-centered designs. However, empathy is not always something that comes naturally. It is a skill that can be developed and grown over time. In this blog post, we’ll explore some ways to grow your empathy skills as a UI/UX designer.

One of the most effective ways to grow your empathy skills is to spend time with your users. Conducting user research and user testing is a great way to gain insight into the needs, behaviors, and pain points of your users. By observing users in their natural environment, you can gain a deeper understanding of how they interact with products and services, and identify areas where design improvements can be made.

Another way to grow your empathy skills is to actively practice perspective-taking. This means putting yourself in the shoes of your users and trying to understand their point of view. This can be done by conducting user research, reading user feedback, or even just imagining yourself as a user.

Another way to grow your empathy skills is to expose yourself to diverse perspectives and cultures. By interacting with people from different backgrounds and cultures, you can gain a broader understanding of the world and the different ways people think and behave.

You can also read books, articles and watch videos about empathy, self-awareness and emotional intelligence. These resources can help you to understand the concept of empathy, and give you tips and techniques for developing empathy in your own life.

Keep in mind that empathy is not something that can be learned overnight. It is a skill that requires consistent practice and effort. Keep working at it, and you will find that your empathy skills will grow over time.

Last, empathy is a crucial skill for UI/UX designers as it allows us to create better, more user-centered designs. By conducting user research, practicing perspective-taking, exposing ourselves to diverse perspectives and cultures, reading and learning about empathy, and consistent practice, we can grow our empathy skills and become better designers.

paragraphs: A design system is a collection of reusable components and guidelines for creating consistent, user-centered designs across a product or organization. These components can include things like typography, color palettes, buttons, forms, and navigation elements, as well as guidelines for things like accessibility, responsive design, and user research. Having a design system in place helps to ensure that all designs are cohesive, efficient to implement, and easy to maintain, and also helps to improve the overall user experience. Additionally, a design system can also be used as a tool for collaboration and communication among cross-functional teams, including designers, developers, and product managers.

The need for a design system arises from the need to create a consistent and cohesive user experience across a product or organization. A design system helps to ensure that all designs are aligned with the overall brand and user experience goals, making it easier for users to navigate and understand the product.

To improve the user experience, a design system also helps to improve the efficiency and maintainability of the design and development process. By using reusable components and guidelines, designers and developers can work more efficiently and make changes more easily. This can save time and resources, and also help to ensure that updates and new features are consistent with the existing design.

Another benefit of having a design system is it helps to improve collaboration and communication among cross-functional teams. A design system can serve as a shared language and tool for designers, developers, and product managers to use when discussing and implementing designs. This can help to ensure that everyone is on the same page, and that the final product is aligned with the overall goals and vision of the organization.
Design systems and component libraries are related but distinct concepts.

A design system is a collection of reusable components and guidelines that are used to create consistent and cohesive user experiences across a product or organization. It includes not only the visual elements, but also guidelines for things like accessibility, responsive design, and user research. It defines the overall aesthetic and visual language of the product and helps to align the design and development process with the organization’s goals and vision.

A component library, on the other hand, is a collection of reusable code components that can be used to build a product. It contains the code for the various elements of the product, such as buttons, forms, and navigation elements. It is used by developers to quickly and easily implement designs, and to ensure consistency across the product.

In summary, a design system is a holistic approach that encompasses not only the visual elements but also the guidelines, principles and best practices for creating a consistent and cohesive user experience, while a component library is a collection of reusable code components used to build a product. While they are related, a design system will contain a component library as part of it but not vice versa.

Atomic Design is a methodology for creating reusable and modular design systems. It was first introduced by Brad Frost, a web designer and developer, in 2013. The methodology is based on the idea that design can be broken down into smaller, reusable “atoms” that can be combined to create larger and more complex “molecules” and “organisms.”
Atomic Design is divided into five main levels:
Atoms: The smallest building blocks of the design, such as individual form fields, buttons, and icons.
Molecules: Combinations of atoms that form a distinct, meaningful piece of the design, such as a form or a navigation menu.
Organisms: Combinations of molecules that form larger, more complex pieces of the design, such as a header or footer.
Templates: Combinations of organisms that form the layout and structure of the design.
Pages: The final, fully-realized design, that are specific instances of templates, filled with real content.

The Atomic Design methodology helps to ensure that all designs are consistent, modular, and easy to maintain. It also promotes collaboration and communication among cross-functional teams, as all members can understand and work with the same set of atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages. Additionally, it allows teams to build and test design components in isolation, before integrating them into larger systems, resulting in a more efficient development process.You can read https://atomicdesign.bradfrost.com/chapter-2/ for the complete reference.

paragraphs: Problem-solving is a key skill for any designer, and that there are several ways to exercise and improve this skill.

First, I would recommend setting aside time each day to work on design challenges and exercises. This can be done by sketching new ideas, brainstorming solutions to design problems, or working on real-world design projects. The key is to push yourself to think creatively and come up with unique solutions.

Second, I would recommend seeking out diverse perspectives and exposing yourself to different ideas and design approaches. This can be done by interacting with people from different backgrounds and cultures, reading design books and articles, or visiting museums and design exhibitions. By gaining a broader understanding of the world and the different ways people think and solve problems, you can come up with more innovative solutions to design problems.

Third, I would recommend learning about and studying different problem-solving methodologies such as design thinking, SCAMPER, or lateral thinking. These methods can provide a structured approach to problem-solving, and help you to think more creatively and come up with unique solutions.

I would recommend working in a team. Collaborating with others can help you to bounce ideas off of each other, and to gain new perspectives on design problems. It also allows you to learn from others’ problem-solving techniques and approaches.

paragraphs: Design systems help startups innovate more effectively, scale products faster, and launch services more easily. It is of great value to both developers and non-developers as it reduces time to market and provides design principles that are consistent, shared, usable, and testable across products. It saves the developer and her UX a lot of time and improves developer morale. The benefits of design systems are not limited to small startups. It is easy for large organizations to design, test, launch and sell digital services and products. Building an effective design system team involves several key steps:

Defining the goals and objectives of the design system is an important step in the process of building an effective design system. The goals and objectives will serve as a roadmap for the design system and help to ensure that everyone on the team is working towards the same end goal.
Some possible goals and objectives for a design system could include:
Creating a consistent and cohesive user experience across the product or organization.
Improving the efficiency and maintainability of the design and development process.
Promoting collaboration and communication among cross-functional teams.
Ensuring that all designs are aligned with the overall brand and user experience goals.
Improving scalability and adaptability of the design
Improving the performance of the product

Specific goals and objectives of a design system will depend on the needs of the organization and its users. They should be clear, measurable, and achievable. They should be reviewed and updated regularly to ensure that they continue to align with the organization’s goals and the needs of its users.
By defining the roles and responsibilities of each team member, it can help ensure that everyone knows what is expected of them and can work effectively together.
When building a design system, some possible roles and responsibilities could include:
Design System Lead: This person is responsible for overseeing the entire design system process and ensuring that it aligns with the organization’s goals and the needs of its users.
Designers: Designers will be responsible for creating and implementing the designs using the design system.
Developers: Developers will be responsible for implementing the design system in the product.
Product managers: Product managers will be responsible for ensuring that the design system aligns with the overall goals and vision of the organization.
Accessibility and Inclusion experts: They will be responsible for ensuring that the design system is inclusive and accessible to all users.

Having clear roles and responsibilities can help to ensure that the design system is implemented and maintained effectively, and that everyone is working towards the same goal. It can also help to ensure that the design system is aligned with the organization’s goals and the needs of its users.
There are several ways to encourage collaboration and communication among team members when building a design system:
Regular meetings: Holding regular meetings, such as daily stand-ups or weekly check-ins, can help to ensure that team members are on the same page and aware of any issues or concerns.
Collaborative tools: Using collaborative tools, such as project management software or design collaboration platforms, can help to facilitate communication and collaboration among team members.

Clear communication channels: Establishing clear communication channels, such as email, instant messaging, or video conferencing, can help to ensure that team members can easily reach one another and stay informed of any updates or changes.

Encourage feedback and input: Encourage team members to provide feedback and input throughout the process, this will help to ensure that everyone’s perspectives are taken into account and that the design system is aligned with the organization’s goals and the needs of its users.

Promote shared understanding: Encourage team members to share their knowledge, skills, and best practices, this will help to ensure that everyone is on the same page and can work together effectively.

By fostering open and effective communication, team members can work together more efficiently and effectively, which can lead to a more effective design system that is aligned with the organization’s goals and the needs of its users.

Research and discovery: Conducting research to understand the organization’s goals, target audience, and user needs.

h2: 🎯 Pixel Round – Making Pixel-Perfect Design Painless in Figma

paragraphs: As a product designer who constantly works in Figma, I often struggled with messy decimal values in layers, frames, and text, especially when preparing handoffs to engineers. I knew this wasn’t just my problem. So I decided to build Pixel Round, a Figma plugin that automatically cleans up those inconsistencies and improves design precision.
Designers spend a lot of time fixing decimal misalignments manually. These small issues:
Lead to inconsistent UI and broken layouts
Waste time on something that should be automated
I interviewed 6 fellow designers and confirmed this pain point was common in production-level design work.
Detects and fixes decimal issues across nodes
Works seamlessly with text, shapes, frames, and components
Provides quick feedback and is easy to use
Solo designer & builder: I designed the UX/UI, defined the plugin architecture, and collaborated with dev friends for QA & feedback.
I ran a quick survey with 12 designers and did 3 short interviews. Key insights:
83% said they often had to manually clean up decimal values.
67% said this slows down their workflow and affects collaboration with engineers.
Based on the feedback, I prioritized:
I kept the plugin interface minimal:
A single pane UI with CTA (“Fix Now”)
Status updates for clarity (“15 layers fixed”)
Toggle to auto-run on document open (from user request)
I had 5 designers beta test the plugin
Improved the error state, added support for hidden layers, and redesigned status messages
Detects and fixes decimal inconsistencies in one click
Helps designers maintain clean files and improve dev handoff
200+ installs on the Figma Plugin Store in the first month
Positive feedback from devs who reported "cleaner exports" from Figma
Saved ~20 minutes per file (based on interviews with beta testers)
Designers love tools that “just work”, so polish & micro-interactions really matter.
Building your own tool gives you empathy for both users and devs.
Sometimes solving your own pain point is the best inspiration for a product.

h2: Improve OTP Push Notification Onboarding

paragraphs: UI/UX Case Study to Improve OTP Push Notification Onboarding at Tokopedia
Role: UI DesignerResponsibility: Research, Wireframing, UI Design, Motion Design Prototyping, UT

Majority of users said that they did not receive notifications on their phones. This is because they don't read the information in the ticker. They also said that the images that appear are only notifications via push-notif, so they feel no need to open the Tokopedia application.
Encourage user to open their OTP notification in Tokopedia apps notification center

Context:OTP Notification is a password code that is only temporary and can be used only once, which will be received by the user through a notification on the user's device.Finding Issue:   User having issue with receiving the Push Notification.Cause:User don’t see any notification on the device.

Scenario:Login on a device that has not logged in to the Tokopedia application using the notification OTP login method.Task:You have two devices, both of which have the Tokopedia application installed. But only one device is logged in.

Result:1. "A bit confused, it's not clear where to open the application (even though it's already listed there).2. "Open the app or what before click send now what after click send now?"3. "Users tend to read information the one that gets the attention first."4. "Directly focus on the banner blue didn't read the instructions."

"HMW help users to show and open their Tokopedia app to check notification center?"- why need to encourage user to open their notification on tokopedia apps?- Issue in tech limitation that otp push notification can’t show directly into user device notification center.- Do we have trick for this?

There are many ways to solve the problem at hand. One way to solve the problem in this project is to use one of the Aesthetic-Usability Effects. Aesthetic usability effects refer to the tendency of users to perceive attractive products as more useful. People tend to believe that things that look better will work better, even if they aren't actually more effective or efficient.
An aesthetically pleasing design creates a positive response in people’s brains and leads them to believe the design actually works better.
People are more tolerant of minor usability issues when the design of a product or service is aesthetically pleasing.

One of the platforms that is used as a reference is Google, especially during the 2-step verification process. The Tokopedia feature being worked on is very similar to the verification flow from Google. Therefore we can take this flow and way of working as a preferred solution option
The reference shot dribbble from Jon Anto inspired me to be able to make beautiful motion notifications

Before making an animation that can solve the problem at hand, I try to make an illustration first using figma to get the composition and components that will be highlighted in the process of making the animation later.
This is the process of making animation/motion graphics, namely by making the prototype first using figma, to get a smooth picture and movement as well as what scenes will appear in the animation.

In the animation stage. I will export the illustration from figma into adobe illustration for later, unfortunately, turn it into an animation in the form of a gif using Adobe After Effects. After being exported into a gif, I applied it to the complete flow of the verification of the Tokopedia apps using notifications that can be seen on Tokopedia's live products until now.
Success to improve the success rate about 4% which translated to remove 6000 wasted request every month or equal with Rp2.1 mio saving per month
Fostering compassion for a user base I didn't know anything about has greatly aided my development as a designer.
Since I designed the project, my understanding of technical constraints and feasibility has significantly increased, and I have been able to set reasonable product milestones.
Rushing to the high fidelity stage could be appealing, but the majority of the work is done before that point.

Game store websites are needed by clients so that the games they make can be published on their own platforms so that they can cut other costs that are not needed in terms of game/game item publicity. In addition, the client needs an admin dashboard for game management matters/game items that will be or have been published.

The primary business goals for the XYZ Game Store website included:
- Having clear ways of locating specific products (game/game items)
- Ability to provide a detailed game/game item page
- Having an efficient journey to purchasing one or more products
- Steering costumer towards popular products

The primary business goals for the XYZ Admin Portal Dashboard included:
- Having clear ways to publish products (game/game items)
- Having clear ways to add, edit, and delete products (game/game items)

In this case, I defined 2 personas. First, a gamer who is one of the potential users for XYZ Game Store, second the game developer who is experienced in publishing games to gain a more reasonable perspective.

For XYZ Game Store:
1. Clear product organization for a seamless shopping experience
2. Product search to easily find products
3. Product suggestions to help in product decision
4. Detailed product information to ensure proper product selection
5. Product reviews to help make informed buying decisions and allow for user input a reviews
6. Efficient checkout process to save the user time and allow for easy purchase of products

For XYZ Admin Portal :
- Easy to add game/game items to publish a new game
- Preview the game before and after publishing to see/review game
- Provide an easy edit feature
- Remove game/game item

To gain inspiration for the game store website, I began by identifying 3 main competitors. The direct competitors I analyzed included steam, epic games, and Ubisoft. My goal was to compare and identify common features across these sites and potential opportunities for XYZ entertainment game store.
The most valuable thing I learned from this was how different websites arrange their games and the layout they use. This was useful information that helped guide the next steps.
From the results of several competitor analyses that I have done, I have gained some insights to serve as a reference source in the process of making features for concept tests, which are as follows:
Games are collected into one section based on the category.
Examples of 10 genres that can be implemented for the initial stage are Action, Adventure, Card Game,
Casual, City Builder, Comedy, Exploration, Fighting, First Person, and MOBA.

The search feature is divided into 2, namely the global search feature with the result recommendation/auto-suggestion feature and the other one searches as a keyword that helps filter games on a page.
Several game recommendation sections can be implemented such as Holiday Sale, Top Seller, Most
Played, Top Upcoming Wishlist, New Releases, Coming Soon, Recently uploaded, and others.
Other filters that can be implemented such as game price ranges.
Each game store has a wishlist and cart feature that will make it easier for users to store goods and check out the games they want to buy.
Each game can be shared using the share button.

I kept the homepage simple to avoid overwhelming users when they first visit the site. To help users easily find products, I included global and secondary navigation, as well as a search bar. The carousel event is one of the most important sections to engage users and can increase user retention and also increase user engagement.

On a game detail page, I like to provide a detailed game description so that users can make sure the game meets their expectations. To make the checkout process as efficient as possible, I provide three options: “Buy,” which allows users to directly purchase the game by first creating an account and then making a payment; “Add to cart,” which allows users to add the game to their cart to purchase later; and “Add to wishlist,” which allows users to save the game for later without committing to a purchase.

On the cart page, users can see all the games they want to purchase. When the user clicks the checkout button, those who are not logged in will be redirected to log in, while those who are logged in will be taken to a page to select a payment method.

If a user tries to check out without being logged in, the system will redirect them to sign in. If the user selects the option to sign in with Google, the system will check if their account is registered in the database. If it is not, the user will be directed to complete a registration form.

After a user successfully registers, they are taken to the checkout page to complete their purchase. On this page, they can see the games they have selected and any discounts they are eligible for. The user is then prompted to pay with a credit card. If they do not have a credit card, an option to choose an alternative payment method is provided.

Once the payment has been processed successfully, the user can access a download button to obtain the game. If the user clicks the “download now” button, they will be taken to the library page where they can track the progress of the download.
My library is a place where user can see their purchased product and also see the download progress.

I did a concept test with 2 people and had them go through 3 different scenarios to imagine they were my user personas. These 3 scenarios included:

1. You want to play the latest game. Try to show me how you find/select games and buy them successfully.
2. Show me how you save the product and then buy all the product.
3. Show me how you buy one of the items.

Users prefer game sections that are stacked or displayed many at once rather than having to see one by one in a carousel via the chevron button.
Users are more interested in video clips than static images when the game card is hovered over by the cursor.
When the product game that is on the wishlist is already in the cart, you should use “in cart” for the title.
It is very important that there is a recommendation section that contains a collection of game recommendations that have a similar category to those that have been purchased by the user.
Reviews or ratings from trusted websites or users who write reviews with playtime data displayed have more than 80% influence on helping the user’s decision when they want to buy a game.
Checkout flow is already good and effective enough for the user.
The filter on the right is too overwhelming, it’s best to keep it as minimal as possible.
Change the download button on the game detail page to “Get It” / “Get Now”. Because the words “Download” can be misunderstood because users don’t download games on their devices.

Facilitate the publishing process which is currently still a bit complicated.
Make the product publish form as attractive as possible so that publishers are enthusiastic about uploading products.

The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a commonly used tool in usability testing to measure the overall usability of a system or product. The score can be used to identify areas for improvement in the design of the system and to compare the usability of different systems or products.
